arc.statement: The PhD is lightweight perception for aerial robots: one camera, one network predicting depth, semantics, surface normals and edges together, and those predictions driving mapping and autonomous exploration on the drone's own compute, in real time.

actOne.title: Structuring the seen
actOne.line: Building metric-semantic hierarchical 3D scene graphs from a single camera and an IMU, in real time.
actOne.label: Part I
actOne.subtitle: Understanding space
actOne.homeLine: Learned depth and semantics feed a visual-inertial estimator, and the map that comes out is layered: mesh, objects, places, rooms, building. Four papers, from showing it was possible to closing the loop back into the estimator.

actTwo.title: Exploring the unseen
actTwo.line: A learned agent over a persistent belief graph of places, open ends and unfinished obligations, choosing where to look next in a building it has never seen.
actTwo.honesty: The formulation and the layering contract are written up. The experiments are not run yet.
actTwo.label: Part II
actTwo.subtitle: Learning to explore
actTwo.homeLine: The agent's state is a belief graph, not a snapshot of the map: places it has been, open ends where its knowledge stops, and obligations it has not yet discharged, with every edge keyed to a route that has been certified. A transformer proposes up to eight options over that graph and scores each one by a distributional model of what it would produce. Certification stays outside the network, so the learned layer re-orders admitted options and never commands motion.

arc.prologue: The same question was asked at Peradeniya in 2017: an autonomous exploration planning strategy for a robot mapping an unknown space, using a laser range finder fused with stereo cameras. It is being asked again 10 years later with a learned model and a single camera.
arc.partsNote: Named after the thesis title, Structuring the Seen, Exploring the Unseen, and matching the Part I and Part II division the thesis itself uses.

story.heading: What I work on
paragraphs: A robot inspecting a bridge, counting warehouse stock, or entering a building after an incident needs more than a point cloud. A point cloud says where surfaces are. It does not say that this is a room, that is a doorway, and there is a fire extinguisher on the wall. Planning, search, and spoken instructions all need objects, places, and rooms.

The sensor is one camera and an IMU: passive, light, inexpensive, information-rich, and geometrically ambiguous, because a single image cannot tell you scale. Every hard problem here follows from choosing not to carry a depth sensor. The reason to accept that is payload, which sets what a small drone can do and how long it can fly.

The thread through all of it is one question: what is around this robot, and what should it do about it? I have answered it with a laser scanner on a ground robot, with a fleet of humanoids in a crowded exhibition hall, and now with a single camera on a drone that carries its own compute.

It started at Peradeniya in 2017, on a reconnaissance robot that had to explore and map a space nobody had surveyed. That work fused a laser range finder with stereo cameras and planned where to go next; it became an ICIIS paper, and I built the SLAM side of it.

The PhD asks the same question with the sensor taken away. No laser, no depth camera, one passive camera and an IMU, and a learned model doing the work the scanner used to do. What comes next puts the planning back in, this time learned rather than hand-designed.

home.lede: I’m Bavantha, a robotics engineer working across computer vision, SLAM and embedded systems. I build models that help robots understand their surroundings, and take them from research code to real hardware.
home.stageLabel: 3D scene graph, built live from one camera
home.capabilitiesHeading: From the model to the robot
home.capabilitiesIntro: I work across the parts that need to work together: learning, localisation, mapping and deployment.

capabilities.title: Visual perception
capabilities.text: I develop multi-task networks that predict depth, semantics, surface normals and edges from one image. M2H and M2H-MX are the perception models behind my mapping work.

capabilities.title: SLAM & spatial understanding
capabilities.text: I build visual-inertial systems that turn a camera stream into a map of surfaces, objects and rooms. Mono-Hydra++ connects learned depth with pose estimation and 3D scene graphs.

capabilities.title: Learning to explore
capabilities.text: I’m developing policies that choose where a robot should look next. The work combines imitation and reinforcement learning with a planner that checks routes before they can be selected.

capabilities.title: Embedded robotics
capabilities.text: I integrate and profile the software on the robot. That includes ROS, Jetson deployment and optimising the perception model with ONNX and TensorRT.

home.appliedIntro: Before my PhD, I was the founding robotics engineer at Expert Hub Robotics in Dubai. I built the ROS navigation stack and led deployments of more than 30 humanoid robots across Expo 2020, healthcare and reception sites.

thenNow.heading: Then and now, the same question
thenNow.thenText: An autonomous exploration planning strategy for a reconnaissance robot mapping an unknown space, with a laser range finder fused with stereo cameras. I was the SLAM developer, one of three students on the project.
thenNow.nowText: The same job with the scanner removed. One camera and an IMU produce a hierarchical 3D scene graph of the building in real time, and the exploration policy that chooses where to go next is being learned rather than written.

home.summary: My work spans monocular 3D mapping on a drone and navigation for a fleet of service robots. I’m now exploring how robots can learn where to go next.
home.appliedDetail: I was promoted to lead a team of three within ten months. Alongside navigation, I fine-tuned a thermal face detector and deployed it in a commercial product using a FLIR camera and an Intel NUC.
home.background: Earlier, I worked in chip verification at Synopsys, including on-site support at Samsung Electronics. At Twente, I’ve also designed robotics labs and supervised three master’s thesis students.
home.featuredHeading: A camera, an IMU, a map of the building.
home.featuredText: My PhD at the University of Twente focuses on indoor mapping for small drones. Mono-Hydra++ builds a layered 3D map from a single camera and an IMU, with perception, odometry and mapping running on the drone’s Jetson.
home.explorationHeading: Where should the robot go next?
home.explorationText: Mapping is one part of the problem. I’m now working on how a robot chooses its next route through an unfamiliar building, remembers unexplored areas and returns to unfinished work.
home.explorationNote: This work is in simulation, with no reported evaluation results yet. It uses its own occupancy map and belief graph; connecting it to Mono-Hydra++ is a next step.
